definition: Analogous means similar in a way that lets two genuinely different things be compared, so that one can be understood through the other.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word analogous. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know analogous should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Critics noted that a film director's job is analogous to an orchestra conductor's: each shapes dozens of performers into a single vision.
Two things can be loosely similar; call them analogous only when the match is tight enough to reason from one to the other.
Analogous systems mirror each other point by point; identical ones are the very same in every respect.

Comparable means similar enough to be set side by side and measured — two prices, two test scores, two apartments. Analogous claims more: the things are genuinely different in kind, yet their structures line up so you can reason from one to the other. Comparable items share a scale; analogous systems mirror each other.

Parallel describes things that run alongside each other in matching form — two careers, two plotlines unfolding the same way. Analogous goes beyond matching shape: it says one thing's workings can explain the other's. Parallel lives merely resemble each other; analogous systems let you reason from one to the other.

Akin means related or similar in nature — a loose family resemblance between things. Analogous is tighter and more structured: the two things must line up well enough that one can be understood through the other. Akin notes kinship; analogous licenses a working, point-by-point comparison.

analogous: Analogous systems mirror each other point by point; identical ones are the very same in every respect.
Early electrical engineers faced a teaching problem: current is invisible, and nothing in daily life behaves quite like it.
Their solution was to treat the wire as analogous to a water pipe.
The two systems are different in kind — electrons are not droplets — yet their structures line up point for point.
Pressure plays the part of voltage, flow stands in for current, and a narrow pipe resists like a thin wire.
The match was tight enough to reason with.
An apprentice who knew plumbing could predict what a circuit would do before ever touching one.
The comparison has limits, and instructors flag them: water spills from a cut pipe, while a cut wire simply stops.
But within its bounds, the mapping still earns its keep in classrooms today.
